--- book: Genesis testament: OT chapter: 1 translation: FLUENT status: QA_PASSED qa_scope: structural editorial_status: REVIEW_PENDING publication_allowed: false revision: fluent-genesis-1-11-biblical-fluency-2026-09-10 --- ## The Beginning

v01: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. v02: The earth was unformed and empty. Darkness lay over the deep, and God's Spirit hovered over the waters.

## The First Day

v03: Then God said, “Let there be light,” and light came to be. v04: God saw that the light was good and separated the light from the darkness. v05: God named the light Day and the darkness Night. Evening came, and morning came: day one.

## The Second Day

v06: God said, “Let there be a dome between the waters, separating water from water.” v07: God made the dome and separated the water beneath it from the water above it. And so it was. v08: God named the dome Sky. Evening came, and morning came: the second day.

## The Third Day

v09: God said, “Let the water beneath the sky gather in one place, and let dry ground appear.” And so it was. v10: God named the dry ground Land and the gathered waters Seas. God saw that it was good.

v11: God said, “Let the land grow vegetation: plants that produce seed and fruit trees that bear fruit with seed in it, each of its own kind, on the land.” And so it was. v12: The land grew vegetation: plants producing seed of their own kinds and trees bearing fruit with seed in it, each of its own kind. God saw that it was good. v13: Evening came, and morning came: the third day.

## The Fourth Day

v14: God said, “Let lights appear in the dome of the sky to separate day from night. Let them mark signs, appointed times, days, and years. v15: Let them shine in the dome of the sky to give light to the earth.” And so it was.

v16: God made the two great lights: the larger light to rule the day and the smaller light to rule the night. God made the stars too. v17: God placed them in the dome of the sky to shine on the earth, v18: to rule day and night, and to separate light from darkness. God saw that it was good. v19: Evening came, and morning came: the fourth day.

## The Fifth Day

v20: God said, “Let the waters teem with living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the dome of the sky.” v21: God created the great sea creatures and all the living things that move and teem in the waters, each of its own kind, and every kind of winged bird. God saw that it was good. v22: God blessed them: “Be fruitful, multiply, and fill the waters of the seas. Let the birds multiply on the earth.” v23: Evening came, and morning came: the fifth day.

## The Sixth Day

v24: God said, “Let the land produce living creatures of every kind: livestock, creatures that crawl, and wild animals, each of its own kind.” And so it was. v25: God made every kind of wild animal, every kind of livestock, and every kind of creature that crawls on the ground. God saw that it was good.

v26: God said, “Let us make humanity in our image, to bear our likeness. Let them rule the fish in the sea, the birds in the sky, the livestock, the whole earth, and every creature that crawls on it.”

v27: God created humanity in his image; in God's image he created them; male and female he created them.

v28: God blessed them and said, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Rule the fish in the sea, the birds in the sky, and every living creature that moves on the earth.”

v29: God said, “Look, I give you every seed-producing plant on all the earth and every tree with seed-bearing fruit. These will be your food. v30: To every wild animal, every bird in the sky, and every creature that crawls on the earth—everything that has life in it—I give green plants for food.” And so it was.

v31: God looked at everything that God had made: it was very good. Evening came, and morning came: the sixth day.

## Notes v01–02: The opening can also be understood as “When God began to create …” leading into the following scene. This draft retains the independent opening sentence. “The deep” names the waters already present in the scene; the wording does not itself explain their origin. v02: “God's Spirit” translates ruach elohim. Ruach can mean spirit, wind, or breath, and the phrase has also been understood as a wind from God or a mighty wind. The capital letter is an English editorial choice. v05: The Hebrew says “day one”; the later days are numbered second, third, and so on. The evening-and-morning refrain is intentionally repeated. v06–08: “Dome” renders raqia, also translated “expanse” or “vault.” It separates waters above from waters below. The translation keeps this ancient picture rather than replacing it with modern atmospheric terminology. v14–16: “Appointed times” can include seasons and set occasions. The larger and smaller lights are described by their roles; the text does not name them sun and moon here. v26–28: The speaker says “us” and “our” without identifying the plural referents. “Humanity” renders the collective adam. Verse 27 moves from a singular human referent to “them”; the English uses “them” for the collective while keeping male and female explicit. “Rule” and “subdue” retain the force of the source verbs. v30: The phrase is literally “in which there is a living being/life.” It uses nephesh chayyah, also found in 2:7; the separate Hebrew word neshama, “breath,” does not occur in this verse. ## Vocabulary v02: רוּחַ (ruach) Spirit, wind, or breath; context determines the sense. v06: רָקִיעַ (raqia) Dome, vault, or expanse; the divider between the waters in this scene. v26: אָדָם (adam) Humanity or a human; also used as the name Adam. v26: צֶלֶם (tselem) Image or representation. v28: רָדָה (radah) Rule or exercise dominion. v28: כָּבַשׁ (kavash) Subdue or bring under control.

--- book: Genesis testament: OT chapter: 2 translation: FLUENT status: QA_PASSED qa_scope: structural editorial_status: REVIEW_PENDING publication_allowed: false revision: fluent-genesis-1-11-biblical-fluency-2026-09-10 --- ## The Seventh Day

v01: So the heavens and the earth were completed, with everything in them. v02: On the seventh day God completed the work and rested from all the work God had done. v03: God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on that day God rested from all the work of creation.

## The Garden and the Human

v04: This is the account of the heavens and the earth when they were created. When the LORD God made earth and heaven, v05: no shrub of the field had yet appeared on the earth, and no plant of the field had sprouted. The LORD God had not sent rain on the earth, and there was no human to work the ground. v06: But a flow of water rose from the earth and watered the whole surface of the ground.

v07: The LORD God shaped the human from dust taken from the ground and breathed the breath of life into the human's nostrils. The human became a living being. v08: The LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and placed there the human God had formed. v09: The LORD God made all kinds of trees grow from the ground, beautiful to look at and good for food. In the middle of the garden were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

v10: A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden. Beyond it, the river divided into four branches. v11: The first river was named Pishon. It wound through all the land of Havilah, where there was gold. v12: The gold of that land was good. Bdellium and onyx were found there too. v13: The second river was named Gihon. It wound through all the land of Cush. v14: The third river was the Tigris, flowing east of Assyria. The fourth was the Euphrates.

## Work and a Boundary

v15: The LORD God took the human and settled him in the garden of Eden to work it and care for it.

v16: The LORD God commanded the human, “You may eat freely from every tree in the garden, v17: but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. When you eat from it, you will certainly die.”

## A Corresponding Helper

v18: The LORD God said, “It is not good for the human to be alone. I will make him a helper who corresponds to him.” v19: The LORD God formed every wild animal and every bird in the sky from the ground and brought them to the human to see what he would call them. Whatever he called each living creature became its name. v20: The human named all the livestock, the birds in the sky, and every wild animal. But no helper corresponding to him was found for the human.

v21: The LORD God put the human into a deep sleep. While he slept, God took one of his sides and closed the flesh over the place. v22: The LORD God built the side taken from the human into a woman and brought her to him.

v23: The human said, “At last! Bone from my bones, and flesh from my flesh. She will be called Woman, because she was taken from Man.”

v24: That is why a man leaves his father and mother, holds fast to his wife, and they become one flesh. v25: The human and his wife were both naked, and neither felt ashamed.

## Notes v02–04: The pinned Hebrew says God completed the work on the seventh day. “Rested” also means ceased. Verse 4 begins an account formula repeated throughout Genesis. Its second sentence introduces the garden narrative with “earth and heaven,” reversing the order of the opening phrase. v04–07: “The LORD” represents the divine name YHWH. Adam, “human,” sounds like adamah, “ground.” The link is retained through the repeated human/ground language. The human becomes a living being; the text does not say that a separate soul is placed inside a body. v06: The rare word ed is uncertain. “A flow of water” leaves open renderings such as stream or mist. v10–14: The river names are retained without assigning speculative modern locations to Pishon and Gihon. Tigris and Euphrates render Hiddekel and Perath. Bdellium and onyx are traditional identifications of the materials in v12; their precise identification is uncertain. v17–18: “When you eat” is literally “in the day of your eating”; “certainly die” preserves the emphatic construction. “A helper who corresponds to him” renders ezer kenegdo. The expression names help and correspondence; it does not itself call the helper inferior. v21–24: “Side” renders tsela, which may mean a side or a rib here. Verse 23 plays on ish, “man,” and ishah, “woman.” These differ from adam, “human.” Verse 24 explicitly uses man and his wife; “one flesh” is retained as an image rather than explained away. ## Vocabulary v02: שָׁבַת (shavat) Cease or rest; related to the word Sabbath. v04: תּוֹלְדוֹת (toledot) Generations, descendants, or an account of a family and its unfolding history. v07: אֲדָמָה (adamah) Ground or soil; linked in sound to adam, human. v18: עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ (ezer kenegdo) A helper corresponding to him. v21: צֵלָע (tsela) Side or rib; the precise sense here is debated.

--- book: Genesis testament: OT chapter: 3 translation: FLUENT status: QA_PASSED qa_scope: structural editorial_status: REVIEW_PENDING publication_allowed: false revision: fluent-genesis-1-11-biblical-fluency-2026-09-10 --- ## The Serpent and the Tree

v01: The serpent was more shrewd than any wild animal the LORD God had made. It said to the woman, “Did God really say you must not eat from any tree in the garden?” v02: The woman answered the serpent, “We may eat the fruit of the garden's trees. v03: But about the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden, God said, ‘You must not eat it or touch it, or you will die.’”

v04: “You certainly will not die,” the serpent told the woman. v05: “God knows that when you eat it, your eyes will open, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

v06: The woman saw that the tree was good for food, a delight to the eyes, and desirable for gaining wisdom. She took its fruit and ate. She also gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate. v07: Then both their eyes opened, and they realized they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves.

## The Human Pair before God

v08: They heard the LORD God walking in the garden in the day's breeze. The human and his wife hid among the garden's trees, away from the LORD God.

v09: The LORD God called to the human, “Where are you?” v10: He answered, “I heard you in the garden. I was afraid because I was naked, so I hid.”

v11: God asked, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree I commanded you not to eat from?”

v12: The human answered, “The woman you gave to be with me—she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.”

v13: The LORD God asked the woman, “What have you done?” She answered, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

## Words of Consequence

v14: The LORD God said to the serpent, “Because you have done this, you are cursed beyond all livestock and all wild animals. You will move on your belly and eat dust all your life. v15: I will put hostility between you and the woman, between your offspring and hers. Her offspring will strike your head, and you will strike their heel.”

v16: To the woman God said, “I will greatly increase your pain in pregnancy; in pain you will bear children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

v17: To the human God said, “Because you listened to your wife and ate from the tree I commanded you not to eat from, the ground is cursed because of you. Through painful labor you will eat from it all the days of your life. v18: It will grow thorns and thistles for you, and you will eat the plants of the field. v19: By the sweat of your face you will eat bread until you return to the ground, for you were taken from it. You are dust, and to dust you will return.”

## Clothing and Expulsion

v20: The human named his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all the living. v21: The LORD God made garments of skin for the human and his wife and clothed them.

v22: The LORD God said, “Look, the human has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out and take fruit from the tree of life too, and eat and live forever—” v23: So the LORD God sent the human out of the garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken. v24: God drove the human out and stationed the cherubim east of the garden of Eden, along with a flaming sword turning in every direction, to guard the way to the tree of life.

## Notes v01–06: The serpent is introduced as an animal; this passage does not name it Satan. “Shrewd” sounds like the word for “naked” in 2:25. In v03 the woman includes touching in her report of the prohibition; the translation does not alter her words to match chapter 2. Her husband is explicitly “with her” in v06. v05: “Like God” can also be understood as “like divine beings.” This is the serpent's speech, not an explanatory statement added by the translator. v08: The Hebrew refers to the sound or voice of the LORD God walking in the garden “at the wind/breeze of the day.” The English does not specify a clock time. v15: “Offspring” translates zera, also the word for seed. The Hebrew refers back to the woman's offspring with a masculine singular pronoun; the noun can have a collective sense. This draft retains offspring and uses “their” without identifying a particular later figure. The same verb is used for the blows to head and heel. v16–19: The construction about pain and pregnancy in v16 is difficult. “Desire” and “rule” recur in 4:7. The woman's pain and the human's painful labor use related words. The passage reports consequences; it does not phrase the husband's rule as a command to husbands. v20–24: Eve's name is linked in the narrative with living. God's speech in v22 breaks off before a completed main clause; the dash preserves that interruption. Cherubim are named guardians; the text gives no physical description of them here. ## Vocabulary v01: עָרוּם (arum) Shrewd or crafty; a soundplay with naked in 2:25. v15: זֶרַע (zera) Seed or offspring; singular in form and often collective in meaning. v16: תְּשׁוּקָה (teshuqah) Desire or longing; its exact force is debated. Also used in 4:7. v19: עָפָר (afar) Dust; recalls the human's formation in 2:7.

--- book: Genesis testament: OT chapter: 4 translation: FLUENT status: QA_PASSED qa_scope: structural editorial_status: REVIEW_PENDING publication_allowed: false revision: fluent-genesis-1-11-biblical-fluency-2026-09-10 --- ## Cain and Abel

v01: The human had sexual relations with his wife Eve. She conceived and gave birth to Cain, saying, “With the LORD's help I have brought forth a man.” v02: She gave birth again, to his brother Abel. Abel became a shepherd, while Cain worked the ground.

v03: After some time, Cain brought an offering to the LORD from the produce of the ground. v04: Abel also brought an offering, from the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions. The LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering, v05: but not on Cain and his offering. Cain became very angry, and his face fell.

v06: The LORD asked Cain, “Why are you so angry? Why has your face fallen? v07: If you do what is good, will you not be lifted up? But if you do not do what is good, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you must rule over it.”

## Cain Kills Abel

v08: Cain spoke to his brother Abel. While they were out in the field, Cain attacked his brother and killed him.

v09: The LORD asked Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?” “I do not know,” he answered. “Am I supposed to guard my brother?”

v10: The LORD said, “What have you done? Listen! Your brother's blood cries out to me from the ground. v11: Now you are cursed from the ground, which opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand. v12: When you work the ground, it will no longer yield its strength to you. You will wander restlessly over the earth.”

v13: Cain said to the LORD, “My punishment is more than I can bear. v14: Today you have driven me from the ground, and I will be hidden from your presence. I will wander restlessly over the earth, and anyone who finds me may kill me.”

v15: The LORD answered, “Then anyone who kills Cain will suffer vengeance seven times over.” The LORD gave Cain a sign, so that no one who found him would strike him down. v16: Cain left the LORD's presence and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.

## Cain’s Descendants

v17: Cain had sexual relations with his wife, and she conceived and gave birth to Enoch. Cain was building a city, and he named it Enoch after his son.

v18: Enoch became the father of Irad; Irad became the father of Mehujael; Mehujael became the father of Methushael; and Methushael became the father of Lamech.

v19: Lamech married two women, one named Adah and the other Zillah. v20: Adah gave birth to Jabal, the ancestor of those who live in tents and raise livestock. v21: His brother's name was Jubal, the ancestor of all who play the lyre and pipe. v22: Zillah also gave birth to Tubal-cain, a forger of all kinds of bronze and iron tools. Tubal-cain's sister was Naamah.

v23: Lamech said to his wives, “Adah and Zillah, hear my voice! Wives of Lamech, listen to my words! I have killed a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me. v24: If Cain is avenged seven times over, then Lamech seventy-seven times.”

## Seth and Enosh

v25: Adam had sexual relations with his wife again. She gave birth to a son and named him Seth, saying, “God has appointed another offspring for me in place of Abel, since Cain killed him.” v26: Seth also had a son, whom he named Enosh. At that time people began calling on the name of the LORD.

## Notes v01: “Had sexual relations” renders the Hebrew idiom “knew.” Cain's name is linked with Eve's verb qaniti, “I have acquired/produced.” Her phrase involving the LORD is compact and disputed; this draft retains the reading “with the LORD's help.” v04–07: The text reports favor toward Abel and his offering without explicitly stating why Cain's offering was not regarded. “Lifted up” in v07 may refer to acceptance or the lifting of the fallen face. Sin is pictured as crouching. “You must rule” may also be read “you can/will rule.” Desire and rule echo 3:16. v08: The pinned Hebrew says Cain spoke to Abel but does not give the words he spoke. No invitation to the field has been supplied in the main text. v11–15: “Cursed from the ground” can suggest separation from the ground or a curse operating through it. The word rendered “punishment” in v13 can also mean guilt; the statement may be heard as more than a protest about consequences. The sign given to Cain is not described and is not identified with race or skin color. v16–22: Nod is linked in sound with wandering. The genealogy names ancestry in occupations as well as family lines. The metalworking phrase in v22 is difficult; it is rendered broadly as forging bronze and iron tools, without specifying weapons. v23–26: Lamech's poem is rendered as a completed-action boast; its verbal force has also been read conditionally. It escalates sevenfold vengeance to seventy-sevenfold. Seth's name is linked to “appointed.” The concluding statement uses the traditional “people began calling” reading. ## Vocabulary v01: יָדַע (yada) Know; in this context an idiom for sexual relations. v07: חַטָּאת (chatta't) Sin; here personified as crouching at a door. v09: שָׁמַר (shamar) Guard or keep; the same root used for keeping the garden in 2:15. v13: עָוֹן (avon) Wrongdoing, guilt, or its punishment. v15: אוֹת (ot) Sign; also used of the covenant sign in chapter 9.

--- book: Genesis testament: OT chapter: 5 translation: FLUENT status: QA_PASSED qa_scope: structural editorial_status: REVIEW_PENDING publication_allowed: false revision: fluent-genesis-1-11-biblical-fluency-2026-09-10 --- ## The Family of Adam

v01: This is the written account of Adam's family. When God created humanity, God made them in God's likeness. v02: God created them male and female, blessed them, and named them Humanity on the day they were created.

v03: At 130 years old, Adam became the father of a son in his likeness, bearing his image. He named him Seth. v04: After Seth's birth, Adam lived another 800 years and had other sons and daughters. v05: Adam lived 930 years in all. Then he died.

## The Generations Continue

v06: Seth was 105 years old when he became the father of Enosh. v07: After Enosh's birth, Seth lived another 807 years and had other sons and daughters. v08: Seth lived 912 years in all. Then he died.

v09: Enosh was 90 years old when he became the father of Kenan. v10: After Kenan's birth, Enosh lived another 815 years and had other sons and daughters. v11: Enosh lived 905 years in all. Then he died.

v12: Kenan was 70 years old when he became the father of Mahalalel. v13: After Mahalalel's birth, Kenan lived another 840 years and had other sons and daughters. v14: Kenan lived 910 years in all. Then he died.

v15: Mahalalel was 65 years old when he became the father of Jared. v16: After Jared's birth, Mahalalel lived another 830 years and had other sons and daughters. v17: Mahalalel lived 895 years in all. Then he died.

v18: Jared was 162 years old when he became the father of Enoch. v19: After Enoch's birth, Jared lived another 800 years and had other sons and daughters. v20: Jared lived 962 years in all. Then he died.

## Enoch Walks with God

v21: Enoch was 65 years old when he became the father of Methuselah. v22: After Methuselah's birth, Enoch walked with God for 300 years and had other sons and daughters. v23: Enoch lived 365 years in all. v24: Enoch walked with God. Then he was no longer there, because God took him.

## From Methuselah to Noah

v25: Methuselah was 187 years old when he became the father of Lamech. v26: After Lamech's birth, Methuselah lived another 782 years and had other sons and daughters. v27: Methuselah lived 969 years in all. Then he died.

v28: Lamech was 182 years old when he became the father of a son. v29: He named him Noah, saying, “He will bring us relief from our work and the painful labor of our hands on the ground the LORD has cursed.” v30: After Noah's birth, Lamech lived another 595 years and had other sons and daughters. v31: Lamech lived 777 years in all. Then he died.

v32: After Noah reached 500 years of age, he became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

## Notes v01–05: Adam can name a person or humanity. The image and likeness language recalls 1:26–27. The ages follow the pinned Hebrew and are not converted into a modern chronology or explained as another unit of time. v06–24: The repeated pattern gives an age at fatherhood, later years and other children, a total lifespan, and death. Enoch's entry changes that pattern: he walks with God and is taken by God. The passage does not supply a destination or a mechanism. v29–32: Noah's name is associated in the saying with relief from painful labor, though the name and the verb are not the same Hebrew root. Verse 32 introduces three sons after an age statement; it need not mean all three were born at the same time. ## Vocabulary v01: סֵפֶר (sefer) Written record or book. v22: הִתְהַלֵּךְ (hithallekh) Walk or walk about; here used in the phrase walked with God. v29: נָחַם (nacham) Comfort, bring relief, or regret, depending on form and context; the regret language returns in 6:6–7.

--- book: Genesis testament: OT chapter: 6 translation: FLUENT status: QA_PASSED qa_scope: structural editorial_status: REVIEW_PENDING publication_allowed: false revision: fluent-genesis-1-11-biblical-fluency-2026-09-10 --- ## Humanity’s Corruption

v01: As humans began to multiply across the ground, daughters were born to them. v02: The sons of God saw that the human daughters were beautiful, and they took as wives any they chose.

v03: The LORD said, “My spirit will not remain in humans forever, for they are flesh. Their days will be 120 years.”

v04: The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and afterward too, when the sons of God had relations with human daughters, who bore them children. These were the mighty ones of long ago, men of renown.

v05: The LORD saw how great human evil had become on the earth. Every inclination of the thoughts of the human heart was only evil, all the time. v06: The LORD regretted making humans on the earth and was deeply grieved at heart. v07: The LORD said, “I will wipe the humans I created from the ground—humans along with livestock, crawling creatures, and birds in the sky. I regret having made them.”

v08: But Noah found favor in the LORD's eyes.

## Noah and the Corrupt Earth

v09: This is the account of Noah's family. Noah was righteous and blameless among the people of his time. Noah walked with God. v10: Noah became the father of three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

v11: The earth was corrupt in God's sight, filled with violence. v12: God looked at the earth: it was corrupt, because all flesh had corrupted its way on the earth.

v13: God said to Noah, “The end of all flesh has come before me, because the earth is filled with violence through them. I am about to destroy them along with the earth.

## Instructions for the Ark

v14: Make yourself an ark of gopher wood. Build compartments in it, and coat it inside and out with pitch. v15: Build it 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high. v16: Make a roof for the ark, finishing it to within a cubit of the top. Put an entrance in its side, and build lower, middle, and upper decks.

v17: I am bringing floodwaters over the earth to destroy all flesh under the heavens that has the breath of life in it. Everything on the earth will die.

v18: But I will establish my covenant with you. Enter the ark with your sons, your wife, and your sons' wives. v19: Bring two of every kind of living creature into the ark to keep them alive with you, a male and a female. v20: Two of every kind of bird, livestock, and creature that crawls on the ground will come to you to be kept alive.

v21: Gather and store every kind of food that can be eaten. It will be food for you and for them.”

v22: Noah did all of this. He did everything God commanded him.

## Notes v01–04: The passage does not identify the “sons of God” or explain the Nephilim. “Beautiful” follows the source's description of the daughters. The wording “any they chose” retains the taking and choice without adding an account of the women's consent. v03: The verb rendered “remain” is uncertain and has also been understood as contend or judge. The 120 years may refer to a limit on human life or a period before the coming judgment; the translation does not decide that question. v05–13: Divine regret and grief remain explicit. The Hebrew root for corruption is also used for destruction, linking the earth's condition with the announced action. “All flesh” is retained rather than automatically reduced to one group of humans. v14–16: An ark is a large vessel or container; the word here does not describe a sailing ship. Gopher wood is unidentified. A cubit is an ancient length based on the forearm, and its precise size varied. The three stated dimensions are preserved in cubits. v16: The word rendered “roof” can also be understood as an opening for light. The following cubit measurement is difficult. This rendering is an editorial choice and should not be treated as an exact reconstruction blueprint. v18–22: “Covenant” is retained as a recurring biblical term. The instruction names Noah's whole family and the preservation of other living creatures, along with food for both. ## Vocabulary v04: נְפִלִים (Nephilim) A designation left untranslated because its identification is disputed. v11: חָמָס (chamas) Violence or violent wrongdoing. v14: תֵּבָה (tevah) Ark or large container; distinct from the word for the covenant chest. v15: אַמָּה (ammah) Cubit, an ancient unit of length. v18: בְּרִית (berit) Covenant, a binding relationship or commitment.

v03: Jokshan became the father of Sheba and Dedan. Dedan's descendants were the Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim.

v04: Midian's sons were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were Keturah's descendants.

v05: Abraham gave everything he owned to Isaac. v06: But Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines. While he was still alive, he sent them away from his son Isaac, eastward to the land of the east.

## Abraham’s Death

v07: Abraham lived 175 years in all.

v08: He breathed his last and died at a good old age, old and full of years, and was gathered to his people.

v09: His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite, facing Mamre. v10: This was the field Abraham had bought from the Hittites. Abraham and his wife Sarah were buried there.

v11: After Abraham died, God blessed his son Isaac. Isaac settled by Beer-lahai-roi.

## Ishmael’s Family

v12: This is the account of Ishmael's family. He was Abraham's son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's slave woman, bore to Abraham.

v13: These are the names of Ishmael's sons in order of their birth: Nebaioth, Ishmael's firstborn, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, v14: Mishma, Dumah, Massa, v15: Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.

v16: These were Ishmael's sons, named by their settlements and encampments: twelve leaders of their peoples.

v17: Ishmael lived 137 years. He breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people.

v18: His descendants settled from Havilah to Shur, facing Egypt as you go toward Assyria. They lived facing all their brothers.

## Isaac’s Family

v19: This is the account of Isaac's family. Isaac was Abraham's son; Abraham became the father of Isaac.

v20: Isaac was forty when he married Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean from Paddan-aram and the sister of Laban the Aramean.

v21: Isaac pleaded with the LORD for his wife because she could not bear children. The LORD answered his plea, and his wife Rebekah conceived.

v22: The children struggled against each other inside her. “If it is like this, why am I here?” she said. So she went to inquire of the LORD.

v23: The LORD said to her, “Two nations are in your womb; two peoples will separate from within you. One people will be stronger than the other, and the older will serve the younger.”

v24: When her time to give birth arrived, there were twins in her womb.

v25: The first came out red, covered all over like a hairy cloak. They named him Esau.

v26: Then his brother came out, his hand gripping Esau's heel. He was named Jacob. Isaac was sixty when they were born.

## Esau and Jacob

v27: The boys grew up. Esau became a skilled hunter, a man of the open country, while Jacob was a quiet man who lived in tents.

v28: Isaac loved Esau because he enjoyed the game Esau brought, but Rebekah loved Jacob.

## The Birthright

v29: Jacob was cooking a stew when Esau came in from the open country, exhausted.

v30: Esau said to Jacob, “Please let me gulp down some of that red stuff—that red stuff! I am exhausted.” That is why he was called Edom.

v31: Jacob answered, “First sell me your birthright.”

v32: “I am about to die,” Esau said. “What use is a birthright to me?”

v33: “Swear to me first,” Jacob said. Esau swore and sold his birthright to Jacob.

v34: Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew. Esau ate and drank, got up, and went away. So Esau treated his birthright with contempt.

## Notes v01–11: Keturah’s marriage and the gifts to the sons of concubines are reported without a detailed chronology. Isaac and Ishmael both bury Abraham. Being gathered to one’s people is retained as a death idiom distinct from the subsequent burial scene. v12–18: Ishmael’s twelve leaders recall 17:20. The final clause in v18 is difficult: its verb usually means fall, and it has been read as settlement or death. This draft uses settlement with a collective referent and retains facing, recalling 16:12; hostility is another understanding of the phrase. v19–23: Rebekah herself goes to inquire of the LORD. Her compressed question in v22 may concern her condition or her life; the English does not turn it into a full explanation. The final oracle line follows the common older-serves-younger reading, though the unmarked Hebrew syntax permits discussion of the subjects. v25–34: Red returns in Esau’s request and the name Edom. Jacob’s name is linked with heel. “Quiet” in v27 is a contextual rendering of tam, not a declaration that everything Jacob does is innocent. The final judgment that Esau despises the birthright belongs to the narrator. ## Vocabulary v19: תּוֹלְדוֹת (toledot) Family account or generations; the organizing formula returns for Ishmael and Isaac. v26: עָקֵב (aqev) Heel; linked with Jacob’s name. v27: תָּם (tam) Complete, sound, or quiet; its sense is contextual here. v31: בְּכֹרָה (bekhorah) Birthright; the status and claims of the firstborn.

v07: When the men there asked about his wife, Isaac said, “She is my sister.” He was afraid to say, “My wife.” “The men here might kill me because of Rebekah,” he thought—she was beautiful.

## Fields and Wells

v12: Isaac sowed crops in that land and harvested a hundredfold that same year. The LORD blessed him, v13: and his wealth grew and grew until he was very rich.

v14: He owned flocks and herds and had a large household of servants. The Philistines envied him. v15: The Philistines had stopped up all the wells his father’s servants had dug in the days of his father Abraham, filling them with earth.

v16: Abimelech told Isaac, “Leave us. You have become far too powerful for us.”

v17: Isaac left and camped in the valley of Gerar. He made his home there. v18: He reopened the wells dug in the days of his father Abraham, which the Philistines had stopped up after Abraham’s death. He gave the wells the same names his father had given them.

v19: Isaac’s servants dug in the valley and found a well of fresh, flowing water.

v20: The herders of Gerar argued with Isaac’s herders. “The water belongs to us!” they said. Isaac named the well Esek because they disputed it with him.

v21: They dug another well, but there was an argument over that one too. Isaac named it Sitnah.

v22: He moved on and dug another well, and no one argued over it. He named it Rehoboth, saying, “Now the LORD has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land.”

## The Promise at Beersheba

v23: From there he went up to Beersheba. v24: That night the LORD appeared to him and said, “I am the God of your father Abraham. Do not be afraid, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of my servant Abraham.”

v25: Isaac built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD. He pitched his tent there, and his servants dug a well.

## An Oath with Abimelech

v26: Abimelech came to him from Gerar with Ahuzzath, his adviser, and Phicol, the commander of his army.

v27: Isaac asked them, “Why have you come to me? You hated me and drove me away.”

v28: They answered, “We have seen clearly that the LORD has been with you. So we said, ‘Let an oath bind us, you and us.’ Let us make a covenant with you: v29: you must do us no harm, just as we did not touch you. We did you only good and sent you away in peace. Now you are blessed by the LORD.”

v30: Isaac prepared a feast for them, and they ate and drank.

v31: Early the next morning they swore an oath to one another. Isaac sent them on their way, and they left him in peace.

v32: That same day Isaac’s servants came and told him about the well they had dug. “We have found water!” they said.

v33: He named it Shibah. That is why the city is called Beersheba to this day.

## Esau’s Marriages

v34: When Esau was forty years old, he married Judith, daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, daughter of Elon the Hittite. v35: They brought bitterness to Isaac and Rebekah.

## Notes v03–05: The promises repeat language spoken to Abraham. In verse 4, ‘will find blessing’ may also be understood as ‘will use your descendants’ name when asking for blessing’; compare 22:18. v08: ‘Caressing’ renders a verb also used for laughing or playing. Here the action reveals that Isaac and Rebekah are husband and wife. The verb echoes Isaac’s name and the laughter in his family’s story. v14: The Hebrew expression rendered ‘a large household of servants’ can also emphasize extensive work or holdings. The household’s precise labor arrangements are not described here. v20–22: The well names carry the movement of the dispute: Esek is associated with contention, Sitnah with hostility, and Rehoboth with broad space or room. v26: Ahuzzath is called Abimelech’s ‘friend,’ here understood as an adviser or close royal associate. v28–31: An oath binds the parties to the covenant. The visitors’ claim that they treated Isaac well remains their account; Isaac has just described being hated and driven away. v33: Shibah recalls the Hebrew words for seven and swearing an oath. Beersheba also receives a naming explanation in 21:28–31. The two accounts are left in place. v34: The names of Esau’s wives and their fathers differ in 36:2–3. This translation preserves each passage’s names rather than silently making them agree. ## Vocabulary v03: גּוּר (gur) Live as a stranger or temporary resident; compare Abraham’s description in 23:4. v04: זֶרַע (zeraʿ) Seed; collectively, descendants. A recurring word in the promises to Abraham and his family. v05: תּוֹרָה (torah) Instruction or law; plural here, ‘my instructions.’ v19: מַיִם חַיִּים (mayim chayyim) Literally living water; here fresh, flowing water rather than stored water. v28: בְּרִית (berit) Covenant: a binding relationship or agreement, here accompanied by an oath. v31: שָׁלוֹם (shalom) Peace or well-being; here the peaceful departure of the visitors.

--- book: Genesis testament: OT chapter: 27 translation: FLUENT status: QA_PASSED qa_scope: structural editorial_status: REVIEW_PENDING publication_allowed: false revision: fluent-genesis-26-28-biblical-fluency-2026-09-11 --- ## Isaac’s Request

v01: Isaac had grown old, and his eyes were too dim to see. He called his older son Esau. “My son!” he said. “Here I am,” Esau answered.

v02: Isaac said, “I am old now, and I do not know when I will die. v03: Take your hunting gear—your quiver and bow—and go out into the country. Hunt some game for me. v04: Make me a meal I enjoy and bring it to me to eat, so that I may give you my heartfelt blessing before I die.”

## Rebekah’s Instructions

v05: Rebekah was listening as Isaac spoke to his son Esau. When Esau went out into the country to hunt game and bring it back, v06: she said to her son Jacob, “I heard your father tell your brother Esau, v07: ‘Bring me game and make me a meal I enjoy. I will eat it and bless you in the LORD’s presence before I die.’

v08: Now, my son, listen to me and do what I tell you. v09: Go to the flock and get me two good young goats. I will make them into a meal your father enjoys. v10: Take it to your father to eat, so that he will bless you before he dies.”

v11: Jacob said to his mother Rebekah, “But my brother Esau is hairy, and my skin is smooth. v12: What if my father feels me? He will think I am making a fool of him. I will bring a curse on myself instead of a blessing.”

v13: His mother answered, “Let the curse fall on me, my son. Just listen to me. Go and get them.”

v14: Jacob went and got the goats and brought them to his mother. She made a meal his father enjoyed.

v15: Rebekah took the fine clothes of her older son Esau, which she kept in the house, and dressed her younger son Jacob in them. v16: She covered his hands and the smooth part of his neck with the young goats’ skins. v17: Then she handed her son Jacob the meal and the bread she had made.

## Jacob before His Father

v18: Jacob went to his father and said, “My father!” “Here I am,” Isaac answered. “Who are you, my son?”

v19: “I am Esau, your firstborn,” Jacob told his father. “I have done what you asked. Please sit up and eat some of my game, so that you may give me your heartfelt blessing.”

v20: Isaac asked his son, “How did you find it so quickly, my son?” Jacob answered, “The LORD your God brought it into my path.”

v21: Isaac said to Jacob, “Come closer, my son, and let me feel you. Are you really my son Esau or not?”

v22: Jacob went close to his father Isaac, who felt him and said, “The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands.” v23: He did not recognize Jacob, because his hands were hairy like his brother Esau’s. So Isaac blessed him.

v24: “Are you really my son Esau?” Isaac asked. “I am,” Jacob answered.

v25: Isaac said, “Bring it here so I can eat my son’s game and give you my heartfelt blessing.” Jacob brought it, and Isaac ate. Then Jacob brought him wine, and he drank.

v26: Then his father Isaac said, “Come closer and kiss me, my son.”

v27: Jacob came close and kissed him. Isaac smelled his clothes and blessed him: “Ah, my son’s scent is like the scent of a field the LORD has blessed. v28: May God give you dew from the heavens, the richness of the earth, and abundant grain and new wine. v29: May peoples serve you and nations bow before you. Be lord over your brothers; may your mother’s sons bow before you. Cursed be those who curse you, and blessed be those who bless you.”

## Esau Returns

v30: Isaac finished blessing Jacob. Jacob had barely left his father Isaac when his brother Esau came back from hunting.

v31: Esau too made a meal his father enjoyed and brought it to him. “Please sit up, my father, and eat some of your son’s game,” he said, “so that you may give me your heartfelt blessing.”

v32: His father Isaac asked, “Who are you?” “I am your son,” he answered, “your firstborn, Esau.”

v33: Isaac began trembling violently. “Who was it, then, who hunted game and brought it to me?” he asked. “I ate some of everything before you arrived, and I blessed him. And blessed he will remain!”

v34: When Esau heard his father’s words, he let out a loud, bitter cry. “Bless me too, my father!” he pleaded.

v35: Isaac said, “Your brother came with deceit and took your blessing.”

v36: Esau said, “Wasn’t he rightly named Jacob? Twice now he has pushed me aside. He took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing!” Then he asked, “Haven’t you kept a blessing for me?”

v37: Isaac answered Esau, “I have made him lord over you and given him all his brothers as servants. I have provided him with grain and new wine. What can I do for you now, my son?”

v38: “Do you have only one blessing, my father?” Esau asked. “Bless me too, my father!” And Esau wept aloud.

v39: His father Isaac answered: “Your home will be away from the richness of the earth, away from the dew of the heavens above. v40: You will live by your sword and serve your brother. But when you grow restless, you will tear his yoke from your neck.”

## A Threat and a Departure

v41: Esau bore a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him. He said to himself, “The days of mourning for my father are near. Then I will kill my brother Jacob.”

v42: Rebekah was told what her older son Esau had said. She sent for her younger son Jacob and told him, “Your brother Esau is comforting himself with the thought of killing you.

v43: Now, my son, listen to me. Leave at once and flee to my brother Laban in Haran. v44: Stay with him a few days, until your brother’s fury dies down, v45: until his anger toward you subsides and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send for you and bring you back. Why should I lose both of you in one day?”

v46: Rebekah said to Isaac, “I am sick of my life because of these Hittite women. If Jacob marries a Hittite woman like these women of the land, what would I have to live for?”

## Notes v03: ‘Quiver’ is the usual understanding of a rare word for an item of hunting equipment. The source records both a written form and a traditional reading for ‘game’; the traditional reading is followed here. v04: ‘My heartfelt blessing’ renders ‘that my nefesh may bless you.’ Nefesh can refer to the living self, not only ‘soul.’ The expression recurs in verses 19, 25, and 31. v07: Rebekah’s report includes ‘in the LORD’s presence,’ which did not appear in Isaac’s words in verses 3–4. The report and the earlier speech are not made identical. v12: The word rendered ‘making a fool of him’ can mean mocking or deceiving. Jacob describes how his father might perceive him if he discovers the disguise. v23–27: The statement that Isaac blessed Jacob occurs before the blessing’s words are given. The intervening questions and actions remain in the Hebrew sequence. v36: Esau plays on Jacob’s name and a related verb for supplanting or pushing someone aside. Birthright and blessing are different words and remain distinct; compare 25:29–34. v39: The Hebrew preposition can indicate separation or source. ‘Away from the richness’ is one reading; ‘from the richness’ or ‘amid the richness’ is also possible, giving Esau’s words a different relationship to Jacob’s blessing in verse 28. v40: The verb translated ‘grow restless’ is difficult; ‘break loose’ is another possible sense. The yoke remains an image of subjection to the brother. v45: Rebekah fears losing both sons. The verse does not explain how she expects the loss of the second son to happen. ## Vocabulary v04: נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) Life, living being, or self; here used in a personal expression of blessing. v12: קְלָלָה (qelalah) Curse, set against blessing in Jacob’s fear of being discovered. v22: קוֹל (qol) Voice or sound. Isaac hears one son’s voice but feels what seem to be the other son’s hands. v28: תִּירוֹשׁ (tirosh) New wine, named alongside grain as produce of the land. v36: בְּכֹרָה / בְּרָכָה (bekhorah / berakhah) Birthright / blessing. Similar-sounding but distinct terms in Esau’s complaint. v40: עֹל (ʿol) Yoke: equipment placed on an animal’s neck; here an image of imposed service.

v01: Isaac called Jacob, blessed him, and gave him this command: “Do not marry a Canaanite woman. v02: Go at once to Paddan-aram, to the household of your mother’s father Bethuel. Marry one of the daughters of your mother’s brother Laban.

v05: Isaac sent Jacob away, and he went to Paddan-aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean. Laban was the brother of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau.

## Esau’s Further Marriage

v06: Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Paddan-aram to marry a woman from there. In blessing him, Isaac had commanded, “Do not marry a Canaanite woman.” v07: Jacob had listened to his father and mother and gone to Paddan-aram.

v08: Esau understood that his father Isaac disapproved of Canaanite women. v09: So he went to Ishmael and married Mahalath, daughter of Abraham’s son Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth, in addition to the wives he already had.

## A Dream on the Journey

v10: Jacob left Beersheba and set out for Haran. v11: He came to a place and spent the night there because the sun had set. He took one of the stones there, placed it by his head, and lay down to sleep in that place.

v12: He dreamed: there was a stairway standing on the earth, its top reaching the heavens. And there were God’s messengers, going up and coming down on it. v13: And there was the LORD, standing above it. He said, “I am the LORD, the God of your grandfather Abraham and the God of Isaac. I will give the land you are lying on to you and your descendants.

v14: Your descendants will be like the dust of the earth. You will spread out to the west and east, to the north and south. Through you and your descendants all the families of the earth will be blessed. v15: Look, I am with you. I will guard you wherever you go and bring you back to this land. I will not leave you until I have done what I promised you.”

v16: Jacob woke from sleep and said, “The LORD really is in this place, and I did not know it!”

v17: He was afraid. “How fearsome this place is!” he said. “This is nothing less than God’s house, the gate of the heavens!”

## The Stone and the Vow

v18: Early in the morning Jacob took the stone he had placed by his head and set it upright as a pillar. He poured oil over its top.

v19: He named the place Bethel, though the city had formerly been called Luz.

v20: Jacob made a vow: “If God is with me and guards me on this journey, if he gives me bread to eat and clothes to wear, v21: and I return to my father’s home in peace, then the LORD will be my God. v22: This stone I have set up as a pillar will be God’s house. And of everything you give me, I will surely give you a tenth.”

## Notes v03: God Almighty is the traditional rendering of El Shaddai; the title’s precise derivation is uncertain. Compare 17:1. v11: The stone is placed ‘at the place of his head.’ It may have been used as a pillow, but the Hebrew does not explicitly say that it was underneath his head. v12–13: The rare word sullam may mean a stairway or ladder. In verse 13, ‘above it’ can also be understood as ‘beside him,’ placing the LORD beside Jacob rather than above the stairway. The Hebrew pronoun permits either referent. v14: The promise repeats the language of 12:3 and 13:16. ‘Will be blessed’ can also be understood as receiving or seeking blessing through Jacob and his descendants. v20–22: The vow begins with ‘if.’ This rendering begins Jacob’s response at ‘then the LORD will be my God.’ That clause can instead be read as the last part of the condition, with the response beginning ‘this stone.’ Neither punctuation choice settles Jacob’s motives. ## Vocabulary v03: קָהָל (qahal) Assembly or gathered company; here an assembly of peoples. v04: מְגוּרִים (megurim) Residence as a stranger; related to the verb gur in 26:3. v12: מַלְאָךְ (malʾakh) Messenger; a messenger of God is also called an angel. v15: שָׁמַר (shamar) Guard, keep, or watch over. The promise to guard Jacob is echoed in his vow. v18: מַצֵּבָה (matstsevah) Pillar or standing stone. Here Jacob sets the stone upright and pours oil on it. v19: בֵּית־אֵל (Bethel) House of God; the place name echoes Jacob’s words in verse 17. v20: נֶדֶר (neder) Vow: a spoken commitment; here its terms extend through verse 22.

v01: Jacob continued his journey and reached the land of the eastern peoples. v02: He saw a well in a field. Three flocks of sheep were lying beside it because the flocks were watered from that well. A large stone covered the well’s opening. v03: When all the flocks gathered there, the shepherds would roll the stone away from the well’s opening and water the sheep. v04: Jacob asked the shepherds, “My brothers, where are you from?” “We are from Haran,” they answered. v05: “Do you know Laban, Nahor’s grandson?” he asked. “We do,” they answered. v06: “Is he well?” Jacob asked. “He is well,” they said. “Here comes his daughter Rachel with the sheep.”

v07: Jacob said, “There is still plenty of daylight. It is not time to gather the livestock. Water the sheep, then take them out to graze.” v08: “We cannot,” they answered, “until all the flocks have gathered and the stone is rolled away from the well’s opening. Then we can water the sheep.”

v09: While he was still speaking with them, Rachel arrived with her father’s sheep. She was tending the flock. v10: When Jacob saw Rachel, daughter of Laban, his mother’s brother, and saw Laban’s sheep, he went to the well, rolled the stone away, and watered his uncle’s flock.

v11: Then Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud. v12: Jacob told Rachel that he was her father’s relative and Rebekah’s son. She ran and told her father.

## Jacob in Laban’s Household

v13: When Laban heard the news about his sister’s son Jacob, he ran to meet him, embraced him, kissed him, and brought him home. Jacob told Laban everything that had happened. v14: Laban said, “You truly are my own bone and flesh.” Jacob stayed with him for a full month.

v15: Then Laban said to Jacob, “Should you work for me without pay because you are my relative? Tell me what your wages should be.” v16: Laban had two daughters. The older was named Leah and the younger Rachel. v17: Leah’s eyes were gentle, while Rachel was lovely in figure and appearance.

v18: Jacob loved Rachel. He said, “I will work for you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel.” v19: Laban answered, “It is better for me to give her to you than to another man. Stay with me.” v20: Jacob worked seven years for Rachel, but because he loved her, they seemed like only a few days to him.

## Laban’s Deception

v21: Jacob said to Laban, “My time is complete. Give me my wife so I may sleep with her.” v22: Laban gathered all the people of the place and held a feast. v23: But that evening Laban took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and Jacob slept with her. v24: Laban gave his enslaved woman Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her slave woman.

v25: In the morning—there was Leah! Jacob said to Laban, “What have you done to me? Didn’t I work for you for Rachel? Why did you deceive me?” v26: Laban answered, “In our place, the younger daughter is not given before the firstborn.

v27: Complete this daughter’s wedding week, and we will give you the other one too, in return for another seven years of work for me.” v28: Jacob agreed and completed Leah’s wedding week. Then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife. v29: Laban gave his enslaved woman Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her slave woman.

v30: Jacob slept with Rachel too, and he loved Rachel more than Leah. He worked for Laban another seven years.

## Leah’s Children

v31: When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb, while Rachel was unable to conceive.

v32: Leah conceived and gave birth to a son. She named him Reuben, saying, “The LORD has seen my suffering. Now my husband will love me.”

v33: She conceived again and gave birth to a son. “The LORD heard that I am hated,” she said, “and he has given me this son too.” So she named him Simeon.

v01: This is the family record of Esau, who is Edom.

v02: Esau married women from Canaan: Adah daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Oholibamah daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon the Hivite. v03: He also married Basemath, daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth.

v06: Esau took his wives, sons, daughters, and every member of his household, together with his livestock, animals, and all the property he had acquired in Canaan. He moved to a land away from his brother Jacob. v07: Their possessions had become too great for them to live together. v08: So Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. Esau is Edom.

## Esau’s Descendants in Seir

v09: This is the family record of Esau, ancestor of the Edomites, in the hill country of Seir.

v10: These were the names of Esau’s sons: Eliphaz, son of Esau’s wife Adah, and Reuel, son of Esau’s wife Basemath.

v11: The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz.

v12: Timna was the concubine of Esau’s son Eliphaz, and she bore him Amalek. These were the descendants of Esau’s wife Adah.

v13: Reuel’s sons were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These were the descendants of Esau’s wife Basemath.

v14: Esau’s wife Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon, bore Jeush, Jalam, and Korah to Esau.

## The Chiefs Descended from Esau

v15: These were the chiefs among Esau’s descendants. From Esau’s firstborn Eliphaz came Chief Teman, Chief Omar, Chief Zepho, and Chief Kenaz, v16: Chief Korah, Chief Gatam, and Chief Amalek. These were the chiefs descended from Eliphaz in the land of Edom, through Adah’s line.

v17: From Esau’s son Reuel came Chief Nahath, Chief Zerah, Chief Shammah, and Chief Mizzah. These were Reuel’s chiefs in the land of Edom, through Esau’s wife Basemath.

v18: From Esau’s wife Oholibamah came Chief Jeush, Chief Jalam, and Chief Korah. These were the chiefs descended from Oholibamah daughter of Anah.

v19: These were Esau’s sons and their chiefs. This is Edom.

## The Horite Families of Seir

v20: These were the sons of Seir the Horite, inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, v21: Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. These were the Horite chiefs descended from Seir in the land of Edom.

v22: The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam; and Lotan’s sister was Timna.

v23: Shobal’s sons were Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam.

v24: Zibeon’s sons were Aiah and Anah. This was the Anah who found the hot springs in the wilderness while tending his father Zibeon’s donkeys.

v25: Anah’s children were Dishon and his daughter Oholibamah.

v26: These are the sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.

v27: These are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan.

v28: These are the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.

## The Horite Chiefs

v29: These were the Horite chiefs: Chief Lotan, Chief Shobal, Chief Zibeon, Chief Anah, v30: Chief Dishon, Chief Ezer, and Chief Dishan. These were the Horite chiefs, clan by clan, in the land of Seir.

v33: When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah from Bozrah became king in his place.

v34: When Jobab died, Husham from the land of the Temanites became king in his place.

v36: When Hadad died, Samlah from Masrekah became king in his place.

v37: When Samlah died, Shaul from Rehoboth-on-the-River became king in his place.

v38: When Shaul died, Baal-hanan son of Achbor became king in his place.

v39: When Baal-hanan son of Achbor died, Hadar became king in his place. His city was named Pau. His wife was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred and granddaughter of Mezahab.

v40: These were the names of Esau’s chiefs, listed by their clans, places, and names: Chief Timna, Chief Alvah, Chief Jetheth, v41: Chief Oholibamah, Chief Elah, Chief Pinon, v42: Chief Kenaz, Chief Teman, Chief Mibzar, v43: Chief Magdiel and Chief Iram. These were Edom’s chiefs, listed by their settlements in the land they possessed. This is Esau, the father of Edom.

## Notes v01, 09: ‘Family record’ translates toledot, the recurring Genesis heading for an account of descendants and what proceeds from a family line. v02–03: The names and family relationships of Esau’s wives differ from those given in 26:34 and 28:9. The chapter’s own record is preserved rather than silently harmonized with the earlier lists. v05, 14: The written consonants for Jeush differ from the traditional reading followed by the vowel pointing. The main text follows the recorded reading. v06–08: The text does not name Esau’s destination in verse 6; verse 8 identifies his settlement as the hill country of Seir. ## The Brothers’ Plot

v18: They saw him in the distance, and before he reached them they plotted together to kill him. v19: They said to one another, “Look—here comes the master of dreams! v20: Come on, let’s kill him and throw him into one of these pits. v21: When Reuben heard this, he intervened to rescue Joseph from their hands. “We must not take his life,” he said. v22: “Do not shed blood,” Reuben told them. “Throw him into this pit in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him.” Reuben intended to rescue him from their hands and return him to his father.

v23: When Joseph reached his brothers, they stripped off his robe—the special long robe he was wearing— v24: and they took him and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it.

## Joseph Sold

v25: Then they sat down to eat. Looking up, they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were carrying gum, balm, and resin down to Egypt. v26: Judah said to his brothers, “What do we gain by killing our brother and covering up his blood? v27: Come, let’s sell him to the Ishmaelites instead of laying a hand on him. ## Jacob Is Deceived

v29: When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not there, he tore his clothes. v30: He went back to his brothers and cried, “The boy is gone! And I—where can I go now?”

v31: They took Joseph’s robe, slaughtered a young goat, and dipped the robe in its blood. v32: They had the special robe taken to their father with the message, “We found this.
